lesson.title: Quality Control: The Cell Cycle Checkpoints
lesson.summary: Checkpoints are surveillance points in the cell cycle where a cell verifies that conditions are right, such as intact DNA and completed replication, before committing to the next phase.
lesson.body:
A cell moving through G1, S, and G2 is not simply following a timer. At several points in the cycle, the cell pauses and checks whether conditions are actually right to continue, and only proceeds if the answer is yes. These surveillance points are called checkpoints, and they exist because the cost of dividing under bad conditions, with damaged DNA, incomplete replication, or insufficient resources, is far higher than the cost of waiting.

The first major checkpoint sits near the end of G1, often called the restriction point in mammalian cells. Here the cell evaluates whether it has enough nutrients and energy, whether external growth factor signals are present, and whether its DNA is intact. A cell that fails this checkpoint does not usually die, it typically exits the active cycle into a resting state called G0, where it can remain, sometimes permanently, until conditions improve, or, for many differentiated cells, indefinitely. A cell that passes G1 is essentially committing to complete an entire round of division.

The second checkpoint occurs at the G2 to M transition. After S phase has finished copying the genome, the G2 checkpoint verifies that replication is complete and checks once more for DNA damage, this time damage that might have occurred during the replication process itself. Only if the genome is intact and fully duplicated does the cell allow the machinery of mitosis to begin.

A third checkpoint operates during mitosis itself, at the transition from metaphase to anaphase. Known as the spindle assembly checkpoint, it confirms that every chromosome is properly attached to spindle fibers from both poles before allowing sister chromatids to separate. A single unattached chromosome is enough to halt the process, because letting anaphase proceed with one bad attachment could hand one daughter cell too many chromosomes and the other too few.

None of these checkpoints work by magic. Each one is enforced by specific molecular machinery, most importantly the cyclin and CDK proteins covered next, which must be activated for the cell to move forward, along with inhibitory signals, some triggered by DNA damage sensors, that can hold that machinery in check. When that regulation breaks down, for instance when a checkpoint stops responding to DNA damage, the result is a cell that keeps dividing when it should not, which is exactly the problem at the heart of cancer.
